newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle heads for Florida landing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle heads for Florida landing.

text.p: The space shuttle Discovery was homeward bound on Tuesday, headed for a landing in Florida despite earlier fears that bad weather might force a further delay in completion of the 12-day research mission.
Officials said the weather now looked good for the shuttle's 7:07 a.m. EDT (1107 GMT) touchdown at the Kennedy Space Center.
The shuttle's twin braking rockets were fired high above the Indian Ocean, west of Australia, to begin the shuttle's hour-long descent through the atmosphere.

The $2 billion gliding spaceship was to reenter the Earth's atmosphere over the south Pacific and make a rare southerly approach to the Florida peninsula, passing over Central America and crossing the Gulf of Mexico west of Cuba.
Discovery's crew of six got an extra day in space after their first landing attempt was waved off on Monday because of a chance of fog at the Florida spaceport.

Discovery's crew of six enjoyed their extra day aloft on Monday by watching the Earth speed by 160 miles (256 km) below and scientists took the opportunity to cram in some last-minute observations with cargo bay instruments.
The shuttle was returning to Earth with an atmospheric satellite carrying a bounty of information on the health of the Earth's protective ozone layer.

As well as deploying and retrieving the ozone monitoring satellite, the astronauts tested a Japanese prototype space station robot arm, grew colon cancer cells for medical research, and pointed a telescope at the receding comet Hale-Bopp.
